title: The keys, 1921
hook: the Sikhs won back the keys of the Golden Temple treasury by peaceful protest

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nankana: reformers who did not strike back, at a terrible cost. Today, the same refusal, and this time it wins something.

A bunch of keys on a ring. They open the toshakhana, the treasury of the Golden Temple, where its precious gifts and offerings are kept. In late 1921, just as the new Sikh committee asks for them, an official acting for the British government takes them into the government's hands. On paper it's a small administrative step. To Sikhs, it's a message: you may pray here, but we still hold the keys. What happens next turns a bunch of keys into a national story.
screen: `A BUNCH OF KEYS.` → `THE TEMPLE'S TREASURY.` → `TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT.`

segments.voice: The SGPC had begun to manage the Golden Temple. Taking the treasury keys into government hands said the British, not the Sangat, still had the last word. Sikhs answered with meetings, speeches and refusals, all peaceful. Leaders were arrested, including Baba Kharak Singh, a respected head of the committee. More volunteers stepped forward and were arrested in their turn. The protest spread, and the arrests didn't stop it. In the end the government backed down. The prisoners were released, and the keys were handed to Baba Kharak Singh. Accounts say Mahatma Gandhi sent a telegram of congratulation, calling it the first decisive battle for India's freedom won. In a salok at Ang 1237 of the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru is called the key: the mind is a locked room, and only the Guru's key opens it. That verse is about the inner life, not a treasury. But it points at what Sikhs remember about this protest: in their telling, the keys in the government's keeping were never the real power; the Sangat's discipline was. Without striking anyone, the community won back what was theirs, and more battles were coming.
screen: `WHO HOLDS THE KEYS?` · `MEETINGS, ARRESTS, NO VIOLENCE.` · `THE KEYS HANDED BACK.` · `THE GURU IS THE KEY.` · then, large: `FIRST BATTLE WON.`

segments.voice: If there's a key nearby, hold it in your palm and feel its weight; if not, picture one. Think of something you're working toward that won't come quickly, a change at work, a repair in a family, a habit you're breaking, and on the breath out, quietly resolve to keep going without forcing it and without giving up. If you pray, add Waheguru to that breath.
The keys. The keys of the Golden Temple treasury, taken into government hands and won back by the Sikhs through peaceful protest. Today's word.
Your line: first battle won. The keys came back without a blow. Day nine hundred eighty-six, done.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember the keys affair, the Chabian da Morcha, as an early victory of the gurdwara reform movement, won by peaceful protest; the toshakhana of the Golden Temple is still kept under the SGPC's management.

notes: The carry 'first battle won' echoes the telegram attributed to Gandhi ('First decisive battle for India's freedom won'); the voice gives it as 'accounts say' and paraphrases. Please confirm the wording and source before any quotation.
The handover of the keys took place in early 1922 by most accounts; the script avoids the date, since the index title says 1921. A Keeper may wish to adjust the title.
Baba Kharak Singh's role and arrest, and the release of prisoners: confirm.
Ang 1237 (Sarang ki Var, salok M2, the Guru as key) paraphrased; please confirm the Ang and the attribution to Guru Angad.
'Nobody stormed the treasury. Nobody struck an official.' is a strong claim; please confirm or soften.
The name Chabian da Morcha and the present SGPC management of the toshakhana in howItsDone: confirm.
